summary: ORBIT is an interactive, browser-based space mission simulation and training platform that puts students in command of designing and sustaining human outposts on the Moon and Mars. We developed a 3D planetary explorer featuring authentic landing sites, a modular surface habitat builder, and mathematical engines simulating life support and power grids. ORBIT addresses the challenge by transforming abstract aerospace concepts into practical, experiential learning. Users manage oxygen, water, and caloric burn rates, balance day-night solar battery cycles, and diagnose critical mission anomalies like dust storms and equipment failures through realistic engineering trade-offs. As human spaceflight transitions from orbital stations to permanent surface bases under NASA's Artemis campaign, this project is essential. It makes space systems engineering universally accessible without installations, empowering the next generation of explorers to master the critical problem-solving and resource stewardship required to thrive on alien worlds.

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Project Details

Project Name: ORBIT — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
Team: Primordial Gods

1. Project Overview

ORBIT is an interactive, browser-based space mission simulation and engineering training platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. As human spaceflight transitions from low Earth orbit operations aboard the International Space Station toward permanent surface habitation under NASA’s Artemis campaign and future crewed Mars missions, students and aspiring aerospace professionals face a significant educational barrier. Existing learning resources are predominantly bifurcated between static, passive textbook equations that fail to convey dynamic systems trade-offs, and oversimplified arcade games that ignore authentic physics, metabolic constraints, and life-support math.

ORBIT was engineered to bridge this divide. It provides an accessible, zero-install educational sandbox that places students in operational command of human outposts on the Moon and Mars. Users navigate through destination reconnaissance, landing site selection, 3D modular surface base construction, closed-loop Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) balancing, diurnal power grid management, and real-time emergency anomaly diagnostics. By grounding every subsystem in published space agency engineering standards, ORBIT transforms complex aerospace principles into experiential, systems-level problem solving.

2. How It Works

ORBIT operates as a unified single-page application built on a centralized reactive state machine. The user journey proceeds through five integrated operational stages:

[ Pre-Flight Setup ] ➔ [ 3D Planetary Recon ] ➔ [ Modular Base Construction ] ➔ [ Live Mission Control ] ➔ [ Incident Detective & Evaluation ]

  1. Pre-Flight Mission Configuration:
    The user initializes the mission by choosing a planetary destination (The Moon or Mars), selecting crew size (2, 4, 6, or 8 astronauts), specifying mission duration (30 Sols / Sprint, 90 Sols / Expedition, or 180 Sols / Colony), and setting a difficulty profile (Cadet, Specialist, or Commander). The setup engine dynamically calculates metabolic demand baselines (O2O_2O2​ consumption, H2OH_2OH2​O turnover, caloric burn) and allocates initial logistics capital (Credits and Titanium).
    • Habitat & Command Core: Houses crew and establishes life-support command.
    • Photovoltaic Solar Matrix: Generates power during daylight hours and includes battery buffering.
    • Hydroponic Biomass Greenhouse: Produces caloric rations and supplements oxygen production.
    • Cryogenic Water Storage Tank: Expands reserves for melted permafrost and recycled greywater.
    • High-Gain Deep Space Optical Array: Maintains communications links with Earth.
    • Advanced ECLSS Life Support Module: Recycles water and scrubs carbon dioxide.
      The placement system enforces spatial boundaries, resource costs, and baseline power draws in real time.
  2. Live Mission Control & Telemetry Simulation:
    Once the outpost is established, the user launches the simulation. A time-stepped mathematical engine executes at selectable speeds (1×1\times1×, 2×2\times2×, 5×5\times5×, or paused). Mission Control displays real-time telemetry gauges tracking oxygen reserves, carbon dioxide accumulation, greywater recycling efficiency (70%–95%70\%\text{--}95\%70%–95%), caloric consumption, cabin climate (21∘C21^\circ\text{C}21∘C, 101.3 kPa101.3\text{ kPa}101.3 kPa), crew vitality, and solar flux. Historical consumable curves and power balances are plotted continuously via an integrated charting engine.
  3. Failure Detective & Post-Mission Debrief:
    Dynamic environmental hazards and hardware anomalies (e.g., Martian dust storms obscuring solar arrays, Sabatier scrubber membrane failures, or battery thermal runaway) trigger visual and acoustic alarm states. The Failure Detective modal pauses routine operations, presents root-cause engineering analyses, and requires students to execute remediation trade-offs with distinct budgetary and survival implications. Upon completion or evacuation, an evaluation engine scores the mission across life-support efficiency, power grid resilience, and incident response, delivering actionable engineering debrief feedback.

3. Key Features and Benefits

  • Mathematically Grounded ECLSS Simulation:
    Feature: Implements coupled differential consumable equations modeling metabolic oxygen burn, CO2CO_2CO2​ exhalation and toxicity thresholds (>1.2%>1.2\%>1.2% cabin volume), water reclamation, and food depletion.
    Benefit: Teaches students that life support is not an arbitrary health bar, but a closed-loop mass balance where one failing subsystem compromises the entire mission.
  • Realistic Diurnal Power Balancing:
    Feature: Simulates planetary day/night cycles, solar insolation curves, atmospheric dust attenuation, load-shedding hierarchies, and battery depth-of-discharge.
    Benefit: Demonstrates the critical necessity of energy storage, especially during the extreme 354-hour lunar night or Martian regional dust storms.
  • Interactive 3D WebGL Environments:
    Feature: High-performance Three.js rendering featuring procedural terrain texturing, orbital inspection, and holographic grid snapping.
    Benefit: Provides an intuitive visual context that enhances spatial understanding without requiring specialized graphics hardware or software downloads.
  • Root-Cause Anomaly Engine ("Failure Detective"):
    Feature: Generates context-aware emergency scenarios with detailed diagnostic briefings, root-cause physics explanations, and multi-option remediation paths.
    Benefit: Fosters critical thinking and analytical diagnosis rather than quick-time reaction gaming.
  • 100% Client-Side Architecture & Persistence:
    Feature: Operates entirely within the browser sandbox with automatic localStorage state restoration.
    Benefit: Enables seamless deployment in bandwidth-constrained classrooms, museum kiosks, and off-grid educational environments with zero server overhead.

4. Intended Impact

ORBIT is designed to democratize aerospace systems engineering education for the Artemis Generation:

  • Classroom and Academic Integration:
    Traditional aerospace simulation suites require expensive workstations, dedicated software licenses, or complex installations that standard school Chromebooks and laptops cannot support. ORBIT operates natively in any WebGL-compliant browser without installation, account creation, or external dependencies, allowing educators to deploy hands-on mission planning modules within standard physics and planetary science curricula.
    • K-12 & High School Students: Practical application of chemistry, physics, and thermodynamics in an inspiring space exploration context.
    • Undergraduate Engineering & Space Clubs: Rapid conceptual architecture trade studies and mission setup prototyping for hackathons and design challenges.
    • Public Science Centers & Planetariums: Kiosk-ready interactive displays demonstrating the real engineering challenges of living on the Moon and Mars.
  • Future Scalability:
    Because the codebase is built modularly around a pure TypeScript mathematical core, future extensions can incorporate multi-crew WebSocket networking for cooperative team roles (Flight Director, Life Support Officer, Power Engineer), live terrain heightmap streaming via open space-agency APIs, and dedicated classroom instructor consoles.

5. Technologies and Tools Used

ORBIT was developed entirely as a modern, lightweight, high-performance web software application without requiring specialized hardware:

  • Programming Languages:
    • TypeScript (v5.6.3): Provides strict type safety across simulation telemetry, module data structures, and event triggers.
    • HTML5 & CSS3: Structural foundation utilizing the Canvas API for procedural texture synthesis.
    • React 18 (v18.3.1): Component-based reactive user interface architecture.
    • Vite (v5.4.10): Modern frontend build engine providing sub-second Hot Module Replacement (HMR) and optimized Rollup code splitting (three-vendor, charts-vendor, ui-vendor).
    • Three.js (v0.169.0): Low-level WebGL graphics engine.
    • @react-three/fiber (v8.17.10) & @react-three/drei (v9.114.6): Declarative, reactive 3D scene graph, procedural materials, camera controls, and lighting models.
    • Zustand (v5.0.1): Lightweight, centralized reactive state store maintaining the single source of truth across 3D viewports, mathematical engines, and UI layers.
    • Recharts (v2.13.0): SVG-based charting engine rendering live historical telemetry curves.
    • Tailwind CSS (v3.4.14): Custom aerospace telemetry design system with space-navy, electric-cyan, and glassmorphism tokens.
    • Lucide React (v0.454.0): Clean, standardized instrumentation iconography.
    • Web Audio API: Native procedural audio synthesizer generating telemetry chimes, ambient space drones, and warning sirens without external audio assets.
    • NASA Baseline Values & Assumptions Document (BVAD): Exact daily metabolic inputs (0.84 kg O20.84\text{ kg } O_20.84 kg O2​, 1.00 kg CO21.00\text{ kg } CO_21.00 kg CO2​, 3.50 L H2O3.50\text{ L } H_2O3.50 L H2​O, 2,500 kcal2,500\text{ kcal}2,500 kcal per crew sol) and atmospheric baselines (21.0∘C21.0^\circ\text{C}21.0∘C, 101.3 kPa101.3\text{ kPa}101.3 kPa).
    • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) & Lunar and Planetary Institute (LPI): Authenticated coordinates, elevation ranges, thermal extremes, and resource proximity for Shackleton Crater, Oceanus Procellarum, Mare Tranquillitatis, Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Olympus Mons.
    • NASA Eyes & MMGIS: Architectural design references for intuitive planetary exploration and landing site beacons.

6. Creativity and Innovation

ORBIT approaches space mission training through several creative and technical innovations:

  1. Bridging the "Theory vs. Arcade" Educational Gap:
    Most space-themed software falls into one of two extremes: academic numerical tools that lack visual appeal, or gamified space titles where resources are trivialized. ORBIT creatively fuses the visual fidelity and responsiveness of modern 3D web applications with genuine aerospace mass-balance and diurnal mathematics.
  2. The Failure Detective Diagnostic Model:
    Instead of punishing students with abrupt "Game Over" screens when resources dwindle, ORBIT introduces an educational diagnostic framework. Anomalies pause time and guide students through root-cause analysis—explaining the physical phenomenon behind the failure (e.g., fine lunar regolith abrasive coating on solar hinges, or thermal runaway in lithium storage cells)—and present three actionable remediation strategies with clear engineering trade-offs.
  3. Procedural Autonomy (Zero Asset Overhead):
    Rather than relying on multi-gigabyte downloadable textures or static audio files, ORBIT procedurally synthesizes celestial bump textures via HTML5 Canvas algorithms and generates mission acoustic telemetry on-the-fly using the Web Audio API. This creative engineering decision keeps the total application build footprint under 2 MB2\text{ MB}2 MB, allowing it to load in seconds over standard internet connections.
  4. Multi-Scale System Integration:
    ORBIT smoothly links three distinct scales of space mission design within one cohesive interface: macro-scale orbital mechanics and landing site selection, meso-scale base construction and architectural layout, and micro-scale life-support metabolic chemistry.

7. Design Considerations

During development, the team prioritized several engineering, scientific, and usability factors:

  • Scientific Fidelity vs. Pedagogical Accessibility:
    While orbital and life-support mechanics are governed by complex differential equations, ORBIT abstracts these into clean, intelligible metrics (daily rates, efficiency percentages, and storage bars) without violating the underlying physics. An explicit disclaimer clarifies that models are optimized for educational simulation based on NASA BVAD standards.
  • Universal Accessibility & Performance:
    The application was engineered to run at a consistent 60 FPS on standard school-issued hardware. Rollup code splitting isolates large graphics dependencies (Three.js, Recharts) into separate vendor chunks, and procedural asset generation ensures near-instantaneous load times.
  • Offline Independence & Reliability:
    Recognizing that classrooms and outreach centers often suffer from unreliable internet connections, the application was built with zero external server or cloud database dependencies. The persistence engine serializes the complete simulation state into localStorage, allowing students to close their browsers and resume their exact mission later without data loss.
  • Cognitive Ergonomics & Visual Hierarchy:
    The user interface employs a high-contrast Mission Control aesthetic utilizing deep space navy backgrounds (#080D19), electric cyan focal elements (#42D9FF), and standardized color-coded telemetry alerts (cyan for nominal, amber for caution, coral for critical failure). Typography separates tabular telemetry (monospaced Consolas/JetBrains Mono) from narrative guidance (sans-serif Inter), minimizing cognitive fatigue during complex mission management.
